# Deck Guide: Applebee's EDA (Phase 1)

**For:** whoever builds the slide deck · **Presentation:** Thu Oct 8, 2026 · 5 minutes max, one presenter
**Team track:** Applebee's AI-Powered Fraud Detection · Tec de Monterrey × Sun Holdings × Databricks Data Challenge

This guide tells you exactly what goes on each slide, which chart to use, and why. The previews below are reduced copies. **For the slides, use the full-size files** in the repo at `eda_work/charts/` (2400 × 1350 px, 16:9, white background).

---

## 1. What the deck has to do

The judges grade five things, each from 1 to 4. To score a 4:

| Rubric row | What earns a 4 | Slides that cover it |
|---|---|---|
| Data understanding and context | Clearly explains the dataset, the variables, the source and the business problem | 1, 2, 3 |
| Data cleaning and preparation | Missing values, duplicates, outliers, data types and prep steps, all clearly | 4, 5 |
| Exploratory analysis and insights | Meaningful patterns, trends, comparisons and relationships, backed by evidence | 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 |
| Visualizations | Clear, appropriate, well-labeled charts that directly support the analysis | Every slide uses a finished chart |
| Presentation and communication | Clear, organized, within 5 minutes, with a clear conclusion | Timing plan below, slide 11 |

The organizers' suggested structure is: dataset overview → cleaning → patterns → visuals → conclusion. The deck follows that order.

**The one-line story:** in 2.1 million receipts, void and discount rates barely move by day or hour, but they vary a lot between stores and employees, and the risk signals pile up on the same people. **Risk is about who and where, not when.** Phase 2 turns that into a risk score.

---

## 2. Design rules (keep the deck consistent with the charts)

- **Format:** 16:9, white background (the charts have white backgrounds).
- **One idea per slide.** Each chart already has its finding as its title, so don't repeat it in a big header. Use a small section label at the top instead (e.g. "Cleaning"), and let the chart fill the slide.
- **Fonts:** any clean sans-serif (Inter, Helvetica, Arial). Section labels about 18 pt, any body text at least 18 pt. Slide 1's title can be 36–44 pt.
- **Colors:** use only the charts' palette.

  | Role | Color |
  |---|---|
  | Accent blue | `#2A78D6` |
  | Text | `#0B0B0B` |
  | Secondary text | `#52514E` |
  | Grays | `#888780`, `#BDBBB3` |
  | Money added / money taken off (only) | green `#0CA30C` / red `#D03B3B` |
  | Chart 08's two extra lines (only there) | orange `#EB6834`, teal `#1BAF7A` |

- **Don't** recolor, crop or stretch the charts. No stock photos, clipart, 3D or animations beyond simple "appear".
- **Text on slides:** keep it to a few words. The presenter says the details, and a judge can't read and listen at the same time.
- **No employee names or IDs** on slides. The data has no names anyway, and IDs aren't needed to make the point.
- **Never write "fraud" as a finding.** The data has no fraud labels. Write "risk signal" or "anomaly". "Fraud detection" is fine as the name of the track.
- Add **slide numbers**, and a small source line on slide 1: *Source: RMH Applebee's POS data, 127 stores, Apr 28 – Aug 20, 2026.*
- Export a **PDF backup** of the final deck.

---

## 3. Slide by slide (11 slides, 4:50 total)

Times are cumulative. The presenter guide has the talking points for each slide.

### Slide 1 · Context (0:00–0:20)

- **Title:** *Where can money leak at the register?*
- **Subtitle:** Team name · Applebee's AI-Powered Fraud Detection · Phase 1: Exploratory Data Analysis
- **KPI strip** (4 big numbers in a row, labels underneath):
  - **127** stores
  - **115** days (Apr 28 – Aug 20, 2026)
  - **2.1M** receipts
  - **$99.3M** collected
- **Optional small line:** Dine-in 77% · Delivery apps 12% · Online 7% · To go 4% of receipts
- **No chart.** Rubric row: understanding (source and business context).

### Slide 2 · The data model (0:20–0:50)

- **Section label:** Understanding the data
- **Chart:** `00_data_model.png`, full width.
- **On-slide text:** none needed.
- **Why:** this is the "variables" part of rubric row 1. One receipt sits in the middle; 5 detail tables and 4 lookup tables connect to it.

![Data model][img00]

### Slide 3 · Every receipt balances (0:50–1:15)

- **Section label:** Understanding the data
- **Chart:** `03_check_waterfall.png`, full width.
- **Optional callout in the accent blue:** "99.996% of receipts balance to the cent"
- **Why:** it proves we understand every money field, and that the data can be trusted.

![Money waterfall][img03]

### Slide 4 · Cleaning: what we removed and what we flagged (1:15–1:50)

- **Section label:** Cleaning
- **Chart:** `02_cleaning_funnel.png`, full width.
- **Optional callout:** "Outliers are the signal in fraud work, so we flag them instead of deleting them"
- **Why:** this covers duplicates (229 exact copies removed, 3,545 split bills kept) and outliers (42,291 receipts flagged and kept).

![Cleaning funnel][img02]

### Slide 5 · Cleaning: missing values and data types (1:50–2:15)

- **Section label:** Cleaning
- **Layout:** `01_missing_values.png` on the left at about 65% of the slide width. On the right, a narrow text column titled **"Also fixed"** with these 5 short lines:
  - 11 GB of nested JSON → 7 clean tables
  - Column types unified across 115 days
  - Tips: stored negative → made positive
  - Times: text → real date and time
  - Typo'd labels merged (e.g. SERV ERR / SERVER ERR)
- **Why:** these are the "missing values" and "data types" items of rubric row 2.

![Missing values][img01]

### Slide 6 · Baseline: what normal looks like (2:15–2:40)

- **Section label:** Patterns
- **Chart:** `04_daily_trend.png`, full width.
- **Why:** this is the "trends" item: the weekly rhythm, holiday peaks, and an 18% decline in sales per store per day from May to August.

![Daily trend][img04]

### Slide 7 · The core insight (2:40–3:20)

- **Section label:** Patterns
- **Chart:** `06_who_where_not_when.png`, full width.
- **Optional callout:** "Not when. Where and who."
- **Why:** this is the most important slide. Rates stay flat across hours and weekdays but spread widely across stores and people, and that justifies everything after it.

![Who and where, not when][img06]

### Slide 8 · People: a few employees drive most walkouts (3:20–3:45)

- **Section label:** People
- **Chart:** `08_concentration_curve.png`, full width.
- **Why:** this is the "comparisons" item. 5% of employees account for 39% of walked-out receipts.

![Concentration curve][img08]

### Slide 9 · People: the signals stack up (3:45–4:10)

- **Section label:** People
- **Chart:** `11_signals_stack_up.png`, full width.
- **Why:** this is the "relationships" item. The same employees are high on several signals at once: 106 employees are in the top 10% on 3+ of 5 signals (void, discount, walkout, comp, card tips over the bill), vs about 22 expected by chance.

![Signals stack up][img11]

### Slide 10 · Stores: Munster stands out (4:10–4:30)

- **Section label:** Stores
- **Chart:** `09_store_scatter.png`, full width.
- **Why:** it compares all 127 stores and shows that one of them is clearly unusual.

![Store scatter][img09]

### Slide 11 · Takeaway and next step (4:30–4:50)

- **Section label:** Conclusion
- **Big line:** *Risk is about who and where, not when.*
- **Three short points:**
  1. **The data is solid:** 99.996% of receipts balance, only 229 copies removed, 2% flagged for review.
  2. **Timing is flat:** voids stay between 0.8% and 0.9% of sales on every weekday.
  3. **People and stores are not:** 5% of employees → 39% of walkouts, and the signals stack up on the same people.
- **Next step line:** *Phase 2: combine these signals into a risk score per employee and store.*
- **No chart.**

## 4. Appendix slides (not presented; for questions only)

Put these after a divider slide titled "Appendix". They don't count toward the 5 minutes.

| Slide | Content | Use it when someone asks… |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | `05_weekday_hour_heatmap.png` | "When is the restaurant busiest?" |
| A2 | `07_discounts_and_voids.png` | "What are the main discount and void reasons?" |
| A3 | `10_munster_by_month.png` | "Is Munster high all the time, or was it one bad month?" |
| A4 | Glossary table (below) | "What's a void, comp, walkout, modifier?" |
| A5 | Cleaning decisions table (below) | "What exactly did you clean?" |
| A6 | Method notes (below) | "How did you pick the employees?" |

![Heatmap][img05]

![Discounts and voids][img07]

![Munster by month][img10]

**A4 · Glossary** (copy as a table):

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Receipt (check) | One customer bill |
| Void | An item removed from the order before payment |
| Discount | Money taken off one item or the whole bill |
| Comp | A receipt where food was served but $0 was paid |
| Walkout | A customer left without paying; the server zeroes the bill with a WALKOUT discount |
| Modifier | A $0 line attached to a dish (sauce, side, "no onions") |
| Gratuity | The tip; the register stores it as a negative number |
| Split bill | One table paying in several receipts |

**A5 · Cleaning decisions** (copy as a table):

| Issue | What we did |
|---|---|
| 11 GB of nested JSON, one file per day | Flattened into 7 tables (receipts, item lines, item discounts, check discounts, voids, payments, taxes), plus a one-row-per-receipt summary |
| Column types changed between days | Unified every column to one type |
| Tips stored as negative numbers | New positive `tip` column; original kept |
| Times stored as text | Converted to real date and time; added hour, weekday, duration |
| 3 fields always empty | Dropped: loyalty_id, service_charge, IsEmancipated |
| Employee names, birth dates, payroll IDs | Removed for privacy |
| 1,800 look-alike groups (3,774 receipts) | Compared contents: 229 exact copies removed ($73), 3,545 split bills kept |
| Weird receipts (no items, no payment, open > 6 h, giant, unbalanced) | Flagged, not deleted: 42,291 receipts (2%) |
| Same label spelled differently | Merged (e.g. SERV ERR / SERVER ERR, EMP 50 / EMP 50%) |
| 67% of item lines are $0 modifiers | Labeled every line: menu item, combo part, modifier, free line |

**A6 · Method notes** (copy as bullets):
- Employees compared: everyone with $5,000+ in sales (2,522 people). For chart 11, also 50+ card payments (2,516). Chart 08 uses all 3,183 employees who rang a sale, because it shows shares of totals.
- Every signal is a rate (per $ of sales, per receipt or per payment), so busy employees don't look worse just for being busy.
- "Top 10%" = ranking all employees on each rate separately.
- Tools: Python, DuckDB and Parquet. The whole pipeline rebuilds with one command (`build_all.py`).

---

## 5. If the rehearsal runs over 4:45

Cut in this order:

1. **Drop slide 5** and move `01_missing_values` to the appendix. The presenter says one sentence on slide 4: *"Only 3 fields were always empty, so we dropped them, and we fixed the column types."*
2. **Drop slide 3** and move the waterfall to the appendix. The presenter says on slide 2: *"99.996% of receipts balance to the cent."*

Don't cut slides 7 or 9. They carry the main insight and the "relationships" item of the rubric.

---

## 6. Final checklist before submitting

- [ ] 11 slides plus the appendix, in the order above
- [ ] Full-size PNGs from `eda_work/charts/` (not these previews), not stretched
- [ ] Slide numbers on, source line on slide 1
- [ ] No employee names or IDs, and "fraud" never written as a finding
- [ ] Numbers on slides 1 and 11 match the charts: 127 stores · 115 days · 2.1M receipts · $99.3M · 99.996% · 229 · 2% · 39% · 106 vs ~22
- [ ] Presenter rehearsed twice with a timer, at 4:45 or under
- [ ] PDF backup exported
